en: I am the warrior Sarybai.
Finding no mountain to strike,
Finding no enemy to fight,
Finding no stone for my teeth,
Finding no head to tear away,
I am a bloodthirsty butcher never sated with blood;
Every worthy rival who faced me died,
And I am one of the measureless heroes.
Though I gulp and drink blood,
My thirst remains unquenched.
I am fury itself,
The black eye of the dread destroyer.”
So saying, Sarybai
Struck Jooruker once upon the flank,
Took the blue spear in his hand,
And roared in fury;
The wretch stood against him.
When Sarybai leveled his spear,
His menace split heaven and earth;
When he stood there enraged,
Could the hero-born Külchoro
Draw back even from stone,
Or turn away from death?
He rejoiced at the word “death,”
Revealing himself a lion.
The lionlike, vigilant man
Swooped straight upon him.
Sarybai, son of a monster,
Charged like a boar.
He sprang like a tiger;
Those who clashed with him did not survive.
He arranged all his weapons,
And the cast-iron head, broad as a room,
Of this infidel was made ready.
He had brows like a crouching hound,
And a head as large as a cauldron;
His two cheeks hung loose,
As though two Dungans had eaten their fill.
Upon the infidel’s two shoulders,
It seemed two great birds had perched.
He roared in fury,
Calling all the khans
To come before him:
“Do not come alone—come in pairs!
Do not come one by one—come all together!
I shall strip away your strength
And spill your blood like a spring!
Now I shall take your life,
And make your blood flow like water.
Come with your khan Semetey at your head!
Let no regret remain within you;
Come, all of you, and harbor no regrets.
Let the warrior Seytek come as well,
Let Argyn and Kyrgyz come together.
I shall erase every trace of you,
And smash to splinters
Your villages set in a circle.
I shall seize as my true prize
Your wife, the lovely Aichürök.
Your heroes and your khans—
I shall slaughter you all.
Without quarrel or strife,
Submit to what I say.
Enchanting beauty Aichürök,
If you do not obey my words,
If you do not surrender Aichürök,
Behold, your choro stood thus,
Seeming like a sheer blue mountain.
His Surkon beneath him,
He wheeled about, leveling his spear;
The steed he rode against the foe
He gripped tightly with his thighs.
Its shaft was steel and its point was keen,
A decorated spear with a tasseled tip,
Shining there in his hand.
Such was the nature of that ornate spear.
From a cluster of barberry on Opol Mountain,
It had been torn out by the roots.
The accursed, ill-fated wood
He had strongmen twist;
So that a sword could not cut through it,
He had it wound with black wire,
And bound with sinew.
He had it covered in mare’s hide,
And had Bölökbai fit the haft;
So it would not slip from the hand,
He had its handgrip grooved.
So it might last for many years,
He had craftsmen decorate it.
He had it leveled at the opposing foe,
And had a tassel fixed to its point.
A master beyond all masters,
He had befriended the prophet David:
The lame smith Bölökbai—
The hero Bölökbai had made it.
They strove and strove,
He and David taking counsel together.
When it came to working the bellows,
A levy was laid upon the Kyrgyz,
And bull-calves were slaughtered.
When it came to making charcoal,
Whole forests were destroyed.
He forged and drew out its point,
And, so that everyone it struck
Might writhe and die,
He tempered it in human tears.
He was a masterful man against the foe.
Subduing the whole wide world—
Was he not the choro accustomed to that?
Punishing the whole world—
Was he not the choro who had done so?
Born into this world—
Was he not the choro who had come?
The keenest of sages,
His eyes could see afar.
He had slain multitudes in many conflicts,
And emerged alone from the contest.
His strength was extraordinary,
And he was famed as the sharp-witted child.
That Külchoro was a lion;
How many giants who faced him
Were leveled with the black earth!
While Sarybai stood speaking thus,
The man adept and masterful with the spear,
Full of cunning and fierce in wrath,
The mighty man who spared no one,
Who never drew back from his youth,
And from hardship, conflict, and suffering
Had never once retreated—
He was that dark-gray-maned lion,
Among all souls ever born,
He was that vigilant hero.
Your noble uncle Külchoro,
When the warrior was distressed,
The black-maned leopard,
The spirit of Manas himself,
Made ready before him in truth;
The short-maned gray lion
Seemed poised to tear him open,
Preparing himself face-to-face.
His lashes burned like embers;
His adversary Sarybai
Coiled to strike like a dragon.
His broad front teeth, large as a gate,
Were shattered and scattered like flour;
At the sight, the heart was troubled,
And his numbers greatly diminished.
Almambet’s sword Joikuma—
Encountered by divine chance,
Found upon the open steppe.
Laid upon grass, it set it ablaze;
Whatever it struck was swiftly destroyed.
When brandished with a cry against the foe,
Its edge glowed red with fire;
When swung against a formidable enemy,
It lengthened to forty fathoms.
Whenever it was drawn forth in valor,
It never returned without shedding blood;
Until it had drunk its fill of blood,
It would not go back into its sheath,
Its green-hued edge gleaming.
No enemy who faced it
Ever remained alive.
Such was the nature of the sword.
When swung against a formidable foe,
It satisfied the surging hunger for battle;
The enemy who faced it
Was subdued in spirit.
Behold the sword Joikuma,
Joikuma drawn naked from its sheath;
He appealed to the spirits
Of the heroes who had vanished,
Your warrior Külchoro.
To bring Sarybai down,
He recalled what such an enemy was.
From Almambet, who passed away long ago,
Syrbarang remained as a bequest;
Almambet of former days
Had received Syrbarang as a sacred prize.
Its might was heavenly steel,
A possession of Chylaba,
The khan of Beijing.
In a garden planted in rows,
Beside the Khakhan’s palace,
He had turned from the black faith to the white,
Fleeing the infidels and becoming an exile.
He had it fitted with a black-hair cord,
And approved it for leveling at the foe.
He had it plated in armor,
And, lest it warp or soften,
Had it wrapped in leather.
To strike the enemy without breaking,
Great David himself had tested it.
When he clenched and struck with it,
No opposing enemy remained standing.
When he cried out and thrust the spear,
It split whatever place it pierced.
The foe who timidly received it,
Though clad in armor, died.
Külchoro’s ornate spear
Had singular torment and mighty venom;
It bore the vapor of diamonds and rubies.
Wherever it struck, the wound was no light matter;
It held a dragon’s poison—
Such was the nature of the spear.
Külchoro’s battle-axe—
Its socket was steel and its edge was sharp,
Its haft was overlaid with gold,
And poison was spread upon its blade.
Its edge was joined with steel;
Any enemy it struck directly
Collapsed like a mountain.
When he brought it down with full force,
Not only men, wretches—
Cliffs, mountains, and rocks came crashing down.
The youngest of sixty nobles,
The favorite of Alooke—
The infidel son of Kaldai,
Your warrior Khan Kongurbai,
Had fallen beneath this axe.
Eskara, khan of the Manchus,
Had fallen beneath this axe.
It had dyed its socket in blood,
And was truly suited for war.
When the axe was being forged,
From Khan Manas’s treasury,
When the lamented man saw it,
Did he not unleash unsparing hardship
Upon the enemy?
Not revealing that its master was dead,
Allowing no alien hand to touch it,
Never yielding to a tyrant,
Never giving an inch to the foe,
Did he not unleash
An unsparing tumult?
When the realm was scattered,
When dogs overran the royal camp,
Did it not strike down
Both Ajybai and Kölbai?
Weeping bitterly to the one God,
And setting it aside for Külchoro,
Did not the venerable lady Kanykei,
Grieving and weeping, take it
Away from Talas?
From noble gray-maned Almambet,
Syrbarang remained as a gift.
“It is the inheritance left by my father;
How can I refrain from shooting
At the infidel son of a monster?”
The enraged choro
Was seized by his thirst for blood.
His opponent was Sarybai;
Not a spoonful of blood would remain.
From the noble-born choro’s
Majesty surged strength.
